source.title: THIRTY-SIX UNSOLVED PROBLEMS IN NUMBER THEORY

accepted.question_text: Assuming mankind lasts indefinitely and mathematical development continues producing both solved and newly open problems, does the development of mathematics have a terminal point, and if not, can scientific development continue without bound?

evidence.quote: Considering that mankind will last to infinite, is there a terminus point where this competition of development will end? And, if not, how far can science develop: even so to the infinite?

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to build a purely mathematical model for society, despite the concern that a completely rigid mathematical-cybernetic system might suppress progress?

evidence.quote: And I ask, is it possible to build a pure mathematical model for society?

accepted.question_text: What will mathematics look like over very long time scales such as 1,000 years or 1,000,000 years, including which new branches might arise and which existing branches might disappear or become obsolete?

evidence.quote: How do you imagine mathematics over 1,000 years? What about 1,000,000 year? ... What other new branches will appear? (Some will be ended, out of date?)

accepted.question_text: If Math(t) denotes the development of mathematics at time t measured from the appearance of life on Earth, does the limit of Math(t) as t tends to infinity exist, and if it does, what is that limit? In scenarios involving total self-destruction, possible reappearance of life, or cyclical redevelopment, how should that limiting behavior be understood?

evidence.quote: If we consider "Math (t)", the development of mathematics at a time "t" ... then ... L = lim Math (t) ? ... And if it is yes, what is it equal to?

accepted.question_text: If life on Earth were totally destroyed and later reappeared, how would later civilizations rediscover, rename, and classify existing mathematical results such as Pythagoras' theorem, Euclid's geometry, Birkoff's axioms, and Erdös's open problems, and would mathematical development pass through the same phases again?

evidence.quote: In case of a total (self) destruction and reappearance of life on Earth, how would they call the Pythagoras' theorem, Euclid's geometry, Birkoff's axioms, Erdös's open problems, and so on? Will mankind pass through the same phases of development?

accepted.question_text: Classify all integer sequences {a_n} such that for every index i and for every j,k with i different from j and k, both divisibility congruence conditions stated in Problem 1 hold: a_i is divisible by a_j modulo a_k, or alternatively a_j is divisible by a_k modulo a_i, according to the two cases given in the source.

evidence.quote: Find all integer sequences {an}n0N* defined as follows: (I) ... such that ai / aj (mod ak). (II) ... such that aj / ak (mod ai).

accepted.question_text: For a fixed distance threshold d > 0 and a given plane figure, determine the maximum number of points that can be placed in the figure so that the distance between every two points is at least d, and determine the minimum number of points needed so that every additional point in the figure lies within distance less than d from one of the chosen points. Generalize both questions from plane figures to bodies in space.

evidence.quote: Let d > o. Questions: (a) What is the maximum number of points included in a plane figure (generally: in a space body) such that the distance between any two points is greater than or equal to d? (b) What is the minimum number of points {A1, A2,...} ... such that if it includes another point A then there would be an Ai with AAi < d?

accepted.question_text: Given n distinct digits chosen from {0,1,2,...,9} with 1 < n < 9, how many distinct prime numbers can be formed using all of those digits, and more generally what happens when the digits are replaced by distinct positive integers? Also, for a fixed digit a, how often does a occur in the n-th prime, in n!, and in n^n?
accepted.context_brief: digit patterns in primes and sequences

evidence.quote: How many distinct primes can we make up with all these digits? ... Let a 0 {0, 1, ..., 9}. How many digits of a does the n-th prime contain? But n! ? But n^n ?

accepted.question_text: Given the radical expression shown in Problem 4, find a rationalized form for the fraction consisting of 1 over the sum from i = 1 to n of the radicals a_i^(1/k_i).

evidence.quote: Rationalize the following fraction:

accepted.question_text: In mathematical logic, is every question guaranteed to have at least one answer, and conversely is every assertion necessarily the result of at least one question?

evidence.quote: Is it true that for any question there is at least an answer? Reciprocally: Is any assertion the result of at least a question?

accepted.question_text: Can one construct a function whose range contains all irrational numbers, and can one likewise construct a function whose range contains all transcendental numbers?

evidence.quote: Is it possible to construct a function which obtains all irrational numbers? But all transcendental numbers?

accepted.question_text: Given n points in three-dimensional space with no four coplanar, determine the largest integer m such that among the n points there must exist m points that are the vertices of a convex polyhedron.

evidence.quote: Given n points in space, four by four non-coplanar, find a maximum m having the property that there are m points among n ones that constitute the vertexes of a convex polyhedron.

accepted.question_text: Determine the maximum number of pairwise non-overlapping unit circles that can be placed inside a circle of radius n. Study analogous extremal packing problems for unit circles inside a given triangle, and more generally for planar figures inside a given planar figure and for analogous bodies in space.

evidence.quote: What is the maximum number of circles of radius 1, at most tangential by twos, which are included into a circle of radius n? ... Study a similar problem for circles of radius 1 included into a given triangle ... More generally: planar figures included into a given planar figure. And in the space, too.

accepted.question_text: For an integer m > 5, determine the least integer n such that every set of n points in space with no four coplanar contains m points lying on the surface of a sphere. Formulate and solve the analogous question for arbitrary spatial figures such as cones or cubes, and the corresponding planar version for m > 4 with no three points collinear.

evidence.quote: Let m > 5 an integer. Find a minimum n ... such that no matter how one chooses n points in space, four by four non-coplanar, there exist m ones among these which belong to a surface of a sphere. (b) Same question for an arbitrary spatial figure ... (c) Similar problems in plane.

accepted.question_text: Fix a base b and a finite digit block a_1 a_2 ... a_m. Do there exist prime numbers whose base-b expansion contains that digit block? Do analogous existence questions hold for n! and for n^n?

evidence.quote: Let a1, a2, ..., am be digits. Are there primes, on a base b, which contain the group of digits a1 ... am into its writing? ... But n! ? But n^n ?

accepted.question_text: For each integer k > 2, does the Diophantine equation y = 2 x_1 x_2 ... x_k + 1 have infinitely many solutions in which all of the variables are prime numbers?

evidence.quote: Let k > 2 a positive integer. The diophantine equation: y = 2 x1x2 ... xk + 1 has an infinity of solutions of primes.

accepted.question_text: Let d_n = (p_{n+1} - p_n)/2, where p_n is the n-th prime. Does the sequence d_n contain infinitely many primes, infinitely many factorial values n!, or infinitely many values of the form n^n? More generally, for d_n^(i) = (p_{n+i} - p_n)/2 and for the derived difference sequence d_{n,i} = (d_{n+1} - d_n)/2, do the same infinitude questions hold?

evidence.quote: Let dn be the distance between two consecutive primes ... Does dn contain an infinite number of primes? Does dn contain numbers of the form n! ? But of the form n^n ? ... The same questions.

accepted.question_text: If the points of the plane are colored with n colors, must there exist one color class that realizes every positive distance d by a monochromatic segment AB of length d whose entire segment AB is also colored in that same color? The source notes that an analogous statement would then also hold in space.

evidence.quote: No matter how the points of a plane are colored with n colors, there exists a color which fulfills all distances ... such that the line AB is colored in c and |AB| = d.

accepted.question_text: For integers k,n with k < n, define a decreasing sequence by n_0 = n and n_{i+1} = max { p : p ≤ n_i - k, p is a prime }. Determine the length of this sequence, meaning the total number of terms before the process stops.

evidence.quote: We define a decreasing sequence of integers: no = n and ni+1 = max {p, p≤ni - k, p is a prime}, for i > 0. Find the length (the number of terms) of this sequence.

accepted.question_text: Can the positive integers N* be partitioned into infinitely many arbitrary classes in such a way that at least one class must contain an arithmetic progression of R terms for some R > 3? Determine the maximum such R for which this property always holds.

evidence.quote: Is it possible to partition N* into an infinity of arbitrary classes such that at least one class contain an arithmetic progression of R terms (R > 3)? Find a maximum R having this property.

accepted.question_text: For a rational parameter a distinct from -1, 0, and 1, solve the equation displayed in Problem 16: x a^x + a^x / x = 2a.

evidence.quote: Let a 0 Q\{-1, 0, 1}. Solve the equation: xax + 1/x ax = 2a.

accepted.question_text: If gcd(a,b)=1, how many prime numbers occur in the sequence a p_n + b, where p_n is the n-th prime? How many values of the forms n! and n^n occur there? Ask the same questions for the linear sequence a n + b with a not equal to ±1 or 0, and for the sequences k^k + 1 and k^k - 1.
accepted.context_brief: primes and special values in sequences

evidence.quote: If (a, b) = 1, how many primes does the progression apn + b, n = 1, 2, ..., contain? where pn is the n-th prime. But numbers of the form n! ? But n^n ? (b) Same questions for an + b ... (c) Same questions for k^k + 1 and k^k - 1.

accepted.question_text: For a positive integer n, let d(n) denote the number of positive divisors of n. Determine the smallest k such that the k-fold iterate of d applied to n equals 2. Also, if σ(n) is the sum of positive divisors of n and m is given, determine the smallest k such that the k-fold iterate of σ applied to 2 exceeds m.

evidence.quote: Find the smallest k such that d(d(...d(n)...)) = 2 ... Find the smallest k such that σ(σ(...σ(2)...)) > m.

accepted.question_text: Let a_1 < a_2 < ... be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers, and let N(n) count how many terms of the sequence are at most n. Determine the smallest k such that the k-fold iterate N(N(...N(n)...)) becomes constant for a given n. Also, when a_1 is not 0 or 1, determine the smallest k such that a_k exceeds a given n. Investigate these questions for specific sequences such as the primes, perfect powers, Fibonacci numbers, Lucas numbers, Fermat numbers, Bernoulli numbers, Mersenne numbers, Smarandache numbers, and van der Waerden numbers.

evidence.quote: Let a1, a2, ... be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers, and N(n) the number of terms of the sequence not greater than n. (1) Find the smallest k such that N(N(...N(n)...)) is constant, for a given n. ... Particular Cases: (a) When {ai} is the sequence of primes ...

accepted.question_text: For a fixed nonzero integer k, are there only finitely many integer solutions p,q,x,y greater than 1 to the equation x^p - y^q = k?

evidence.quote: Let k be a non-zero integer. There are only a finite number of solutions in integers p, q, x, y, each greater than 1, of the equation x^p - y^q = k.

accepted.question_text: For a sequence of integers x_n and a digit k between 0 and q, define the position sequence U_n^(k) to record the position of digit k in x_n when it appears and 0 otherwise. Study convergence and monotonicity of U_n^(k) when x_n is the sequence of primes, then for x_n = n! and x_n = n^n. Determine whether these position sequences contain infinitely many prime values, and generalize to rational sequences x_n.

evidence.quote: Study {U(k)(pn)}n, where {pn}n is the sequence of primes. Convergence, monotony. The same questions for the sequences: (2) xn = n!, (3) xn = n^n. Do the sequences of position U_n^(k) contain an infinity of primes?

accepted.question_text: For a number M written in base b, let g(M) be the set of distinct digits occurring in M, let n_g(M) be the number of groups of M each containing all digits of g(M), and let R_g(M) be the number of digits in g(M). Determine n_g and R_g for p_n, n!, n^n, and the radical expression shown in Problem 22. For a given k > 1, ask whether infinitely many such numbers have generalized period length k or number of generalized periods equal to k. For a fixed set of distinct digits {a_1,...,a_h}, ask whether infinitely many such numbers have generalized period exactly that set.

evidence.quote: Questions: (1) Find ng, Rg for pn, n!, n^n, ... (2) For a given k > 1, is there an infinity of primes pn, or n!, or n^n ... which have a generalized period of length k? ... (3) Let a1, a2, ..., ah distinct digits. Is there an infinity of primes pn, or n!, or n^n ... which have as generalized period the set {a1, a2, ..., ah}?

accepted.question_text: For fixed n, determine the largest r such that the set {1,2,...,r} can be partitioned into n classes with no class containing x,y,z satisfying xy = z. Ask the analogous question when x^y = z, and when no element of a class can be the sum of other elements of the same class.

evidence.quote: Find the maximum r such that: the set {1, 2, ..., r} can be partitioned into n classes such that no class contains integers x, y, z with xy = z. Same question when x^y = z. Same question when no integer can be the sum of another integer of its class.

accepted.question_text: Given N = {1,2,...,n}, determine the largest subset of N with the property that no m elements of the subset form an arithmetic progression, where n > m > 2. Ask the analogous question forbidding m-term geometric progressions. More generally, for an m-ary relation R on a set N, determine the largest subset with no m-tuple satisfying R, and study what changes when N has continuum cardinality, for example an interval of real numbers.

evidence.quote: Find the maxim number of elements extracted from N such that any m from these be not an arithmetic progression (n > m > 2). Same question when the m elements must not be a geometrical progression. More generally: Let R be a given m-ary relation on a field N. What is the maximum number of elements extracted from N such that any m from these be not in this relation?

accepted.question_text: Let ω-numbers be numbers of the form a + bω, where ω is a complex n-th root of unity and unique factorization holds. Is the configuration of ω-primes symmetric with respect to the regular 2n-gon?

evidence.quote: Conjecture: The configuration of ω primes are symmetric of the 2n regular polygon.

accepted.question_text: The Diophantine equation x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1 has the nontrivial integer solutions (9,10,-12) and (-6,-8,9). How many other nontrivial integer solutions are there?

evidence.quote: The equation x3 + y3 + z3 = 1 has as solutions (9, 10, -12) and (-6, -8, 9). How many other nontrivial integer solutions are there?

accepted.question_text: For fixed k in the product R_m = ∏_{n=1}^m (p_n + k)/(p_n - k), where p_n is the n-th prime, is R_m an integer only for finitely many values of m? More generally, for which k does no value of m make R_m an integer?

evidence.quote: We conjecture that Rm = Π (pn+k)/(pn-k), with k 0 N*, is an integer for a finite number of values of m. There is an infinite number of k for which no Rm is an integer.

accepted.question_text: Let 1 < a_1 < a_2 < ... be an infinite sequence of integers with no three terms in arithmetic progression. Must the reciprocal sum Σ 1/a_n always be less than 2? Is the map S({a_n}) = Σ 1/a_n bijective on such sequences? Formulate and answer the analogous questions for geometrically constrained sequences, and more generally maximize Σ 1/a_n for sequences built to avoid tuples satisfying a prescribed function relation f(a_{i_1},...,a_{i_m}) = a_{i_{m+1}}.

evidence.quote: Let 1 < a1 < a2 < ... be an infinite sequence of integers such that any three members do not constitute an arithmetical progression. Is it true that always Σ 1/an < 2? Is the function S({an}) = Σ 1/an bijective? ... More generally ... Find max Σ 1/an.

accepted.question_text: Let σ(n) be the sum of divisors of n, J(x) the number of primes not exceeding x, ω(n) the number of distinct prime factors of n, d(n) the number of positive divisors of n, and p(n) the largest prime factor of n. Determine the smallest iteration count k for which the five conditions listed in Problem 29 hold, namely σ^(k)(n) > m, J^(k)(x) = 1, ω^(k)(n) = 1, d^(k)(n) > m, and the repeated map p(p(...(p(n)-1)...)-1)-1 equals 1. Generalize these questions to the variants named in the source.

evidence.quote: Find the smallest k for which: (a) for fixed n and m, we have σ(k)(n) > m. (b) for a fixed real x, with x > 2, we have J(k)(x) = 1. (c) for a fixed n, we have ω(k)(n) = 1. (d) for fixed n and m, we have d(k)(n) > m. (e) for a fixed n, we have p(p(...(p(n)-1)...)-1)-1 = 1.

accepted.question_text: If n(a) denotes the arithmetic function used in Carmichael's conjecture, is it true that for every positive integers a and b there exists a positive integer c such that n(a) · n(b) = n(c)? If so, does repeated induction imply that for every finite list a_1,...,a_n there exists b with n(a_1) ··· n(a_n) = n(b)?

evidence.quote: Conjecture: ∀a∈N*, ∀b∈N*, ∃c∈N*: n(a)·n(b) = n(c). For a = 1 it results Carmichael's conjecture.

accepted.question_text: Although the source gives a negative answer to covering all positive integers by finitely many geometric progressions, it asks for a general criterion: for a fixed n, find necessary and sufficient conditions on a class of positive-integer sequences guaranteeing that n distinct sequences from that class cover all positive integers.

evidence.quote: *Find a necessary and sufficient condition for a general class of positive integer sequences such that, for a fixed n, there are n (distinct) sequences of this class which cover all integers.

accepted.question_text: Consider the linear equation from Problem 32 whose coefficients involve several distinct irrational radicals. What conditions on the parameters m,n,p,q,r,s are necessary and sufficient for the equation to admit integer solutions in the variables x,y,z,w?

evidence.quote: What conditions must the parameters m, n, p, q, r and s accomplish such that the equation admits integer solutions (x, y, z and w being variables)?

accepted.question_text: Problem 33 gives solutions for a specific parallelogram and prism case, but leaves the general variants open. For a given distance d > 0 and a plane figure or body in space, determine the maximum number of points with pairwise distance at least d, determine the minimum guarding set forcing every added point to lie within distance less than d from a chosen point, and resolve the corresponding interior-only, frontier-only, and strict-inequality variants.

evidence.quote: (III) These are generally open (unsolved) questions.

accepted.question_text: For the equation x^y - floor(x) = y, the source provides many solved cases but explicitly leaves two families open: the case y is irrational, and the case y = m/n is rational but nonintegral. Determine all real solutions in those unresolved cases.

evidence.quote: (1) When y∈R\Q the author is not able to answer.
(12) y = m/n ∈ Q\Z ... The author is not able to solve the equation in this case.

accepted.question_text: For the point configuration on a circular disk described in Problem 35, does the quantity n defined there equal the true maximum number of points in the disk whose pairwise distances are at least d? More generally, characterize which point networks maximize this number, and generalize the problem to arbitrary figures in the plane and arbitrary bodies in space.

evidence.quote: Is n equal to the maximum number of points on the disk with this property?* Generalize for an arbitrary figure in plane.** Generalize also for an arbitrary corps in space.**
For which point networks is n maximum? (Here it is an open question).

accepted.question_text: Under the paper's proposed extension of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox, if physical space is infinite, must the maximum possible speed also be infinite?

evidence.quote: c) An Open Question now: If the space is infinite, is the maximum speed infinite?
